executive_summary: The defining thread of the day is the intensifying battle over who controls the future of artificial intelligence, a contest that is simultaneously reshaping corporate power, technological competition, and public trust. The Musk v. Altman trial, now reduced to a raw credibility war between two competing visions of who can be trusted with AGI, crystallizes a broader question that MIT Technology Review's Google I/O analysis reinforces: the AI landscape is consolidating around a small number of actors — Anthropic, OpenAI, and a trailing Google — whose decisions will determine how transformative technology is governed and distributed. The trial's central tension, whether OpenAI's nonprofit mission was betrayed for profit or whether Musk simply wants personal dominance over AGI, is not merely legal theater; it is a proxy fight over the legitimacy of the institutions now building systems with civilization-scale implications. Meanwhile, The Economist's examination of the backlash against data centers grounds this abstract power struggle in concrete infrastructure, reminding readers that AI supremacy requires massive physical investment that carries real environmental and community costs. Together, these stories make clear that the AI race is no longer just a technology story — it is a governance, accountability, and power story, and the outcomes being decided right now will be difficult to reverse.

newsletters.title: 🔴 Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?

items.headline: Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?
items.blurb: A year ago I reported on the impact of artificial intelligence on the fight against climate change. On the one hand, data centres used a lot of electricity; on the other, that electricity was mostly renewable, and could be used to develop technologies that helped cut emissions around the world. Overall it felt like cause for cautious optimism, especially if—as we argued in an accompanying leader—AI companies would share more information about the impact of their systems to help consumers make informed decisions. A lot has changed since then. Some shifts were predictable. The amount of electricity the AI industry uses has exploded. The biggest models take more energy to train and run than they did last year, and they are being used by more people to do more things more of the time. Some adjustments were grimly inevitable. Where big tech companies once felt bound by promises they had made in a different political era to cut, or even reverse, their emissions, they now seem happy to switch on new gas turbines to power their growing ambitions, although they still generally insist that the extra energy use is just a temporary measure to compensate for a lack of capacity on the electricity grid. Other changes were more surprising. Last year data-centre impacts felt like a niche topic discussed by people interested in the overlap between AI and climate change. Now they are an increasingly important part of national—and international—politics. In America politicians are proposing regional and national moratoriums on construction, prompting entrepreneurs to wonder whether it might be cheaper to launch computers into space rather than fight through the morass on Earth.

longform.title: What to expect from Google this week
longform.thesis: Google enters I/O 2026 as a clear third-place foundation model competitor, with a critical coding deficit against Anthropic and OpenAI offset only by its unmatched strength in AI for science.
longform.context: The piece is a pre-conference preview written ahead of Google I/O 2026, responding to a marked shift in the competitive AI landscape since I/O 2025, when Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro still placed it among the top-tier model providers.
arguments: Google has fallen significantly behind in AI coding, the metric now most determinative of foundation model reputation: Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex are 'so dramatically superior' that DeepMind engineers reportedly had to be permitted to use Claude for their own work, a damning internal admission of the gap. A new DeepMind coding team and Nobel laureate John Jumper's involvement suggest Google is treating this as a crisis, with a likely Antigravity platform update at I/O — but the author judges a return to the coding frontier in two days unlikely.

Science and health represent Google's genuine competitive advantage: DeepMind is the only frontier AI lab with a Nobel Prize, and tools like the AI co-scientist (described as an 'oracle' by a Stanford scientist) and AlphaEvolve demonstrate sustained leadership in AI-for-science that receives less attention than coding benchmarks but is 'no less consequential.' The public launch of AI-powered Health Coach at I/O is tempered by its apparent focus on fitness and diet rather than clinical concerns, leaving open whether Google is behind in health AI or exercising appropriate caution.

Google faces internal and reputational pressures it will try to suppress on stage: 600 employees, many from DeepMind, sent a protest letter to CEO Sundar Pichai over a DoD deal that was signed the very next day, and while DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis has avoided the public feuding of Altman and Amodei, the author notes that 'controversies will worm their way in regardless,' testing Google's 'veneer of neutrality.'
longform.significance: The piece matters because it reframes the Google I/O narrative from a celebration of AI leadership to a damage-control exercise, with the coding gap serving as a concrete, measurable proxy for broader competitive decline. It also highlights that scientific AI — where Google leads — may ultimately prove more consequential than coding tools, an underreported asymmetry in how the AI race is being scored. The internal DoD protest and its immediate dismissal raise unresolved questions about employee governance at frontier AI labs.
questions_raised: If Google's own engineers prefer Claude Code over internal tools, how deep is the technical deficit, and can a new coding team close it fast enough to matter before enterprise and developer ecosystems lock in around Anthropic and OpenAI?

Does Google's apparent caution in health AI — deploying a fitness coach rather than a clinical tool — reflect responsible risk management or a failure to compete, and who gets to define that distinction as OpenAI aggressively shapes the health AI conversation?

longform.title: Musk v. Altman week 3: now the jury will pick a side
longform.thesis: The final week of the Musk v. Altman trial reduced to a credibility contest between two competing narratives: Altman as a self-dealing liar who betrayed OpenAI's nonprofit mission, and Musk as a power-hungry actor seeking personal control over AGI.
longform.context: This newsletter dispatch covers week three of the ongoing Musk v. Altman trial, the culmination of a lawsuit in which Elon Musk alleges Sam Altman and OpenAI betrayed the organization's founding nonprofit commitments. Reporter Michelle Kim, who is also a lawyer, has covered all three weeks from inside the courtroom.
arguments: Both sides concentrated their closing efforts on destroying the opposing party's personal credibility rather than purely legal arguments — Altman was accused of 'lying and self-dealing' while Musk was portrayed as 'a power-seeker trying to control artificial general intelligence,' framing the verdict as a character judgment as much as a legal one.

The trial surfaced new internal details about OpenAI's contested nonprofit structure, suggesting the organization's governance and mission integrity are genuinely disputed facts, not settled background — material that could affect how courts and regulators treat OpenAI's ongoing conversion to a for-profit entity.

A detail about a 'golden trophy of a donkey's ass awarded to an employee who challenged Musk' illustrates the internal culture and power dynamics at play in early OpenAI, providing evidentiary color about Musk's management style that lawyers used to support the portrayal of him as a controlling figure.
longform.significance: The case is a proxy battle over who controls the narrative — and potentially the legal structure — of the most consequential AI company in the world, with the jury's verdict set to shape public and regulatory understanding of OpenAI's nonprofit origins. Coming alongside news of SpaceX's imminent $1.75 trillion IPO and Trump's alleged stock trades ahead of favorable tech-policy decisions, the trial sits at the center of a broader moment in which personal power, institutional legitimacy, and AI governance are visibly entangled. The outcome will either validate or undermine Musk's standing to challenge OpenAI's for-profit transition in future litigation and regulatory proceedings.
questions_raised: If the jury sides with Altman on credibility, does that foreclose future legal or regulatory challenges to OpenAI's nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion, or does the structural question remain independently justiciable?

The article does not resolve what evidence, beyond character testimony, was introduced about the actual terms of OpenAI's founding agreements — leaving open whether the legal case rests on enforceable contractual commitments or on looser founding-era representations.
